text_blocks.snippet: Treating high blood pressure (hypertension) usually involves a mix of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, if needed, prescription medications. The standard treatment goal for most adults is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
snippet_highlighted_words: a mix of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, if needed, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Doctors recommend lifestyle changes for everyone with high blood pressure. These changes can lower your numbers or reduce the amount of medication you need:

list.snippet: Eat a heart-healthy diet: Follow the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Reduce sodium (salt): Aim to lower your daily salt intake (ideally under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Exercise regularly: Get at least 30 minutes of aerobic activity (such as brisk walking) most days of the week.
Manage your weight: Losing extra body weight takes stress off your heart and blood vessels.
Limit alcohol and avoid smoking: Cut back on alcohol and quit smoking or using tobacco products, which narrow blood vessels.
Get quality sleep: Aim for 7 or more hours of sleep per night to help manage stress hormones.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes alone do not lower blood pressure enough—or if you have stage 2 hypertension or higher health risks—your doctor may prescribe one or more medications.
The four main classes of first-line blood pressure medications include:

list.snippet: ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril): Keep blood vessels from narrowing.
ARBs / Angiotensin II receptor blockers (e.g., losartan, valsartan): Relax and widen blood vessels by blocking specific chemical signals.
Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax.
Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide): Help your body get rid of excess water and sodium (salt) through urine.

text_blocks.snippet: Other or second-line medications (such as beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, or central-acting agents like clonidine) may be added depending on your age, race, or other conditions like heart disease, kidney disease, or diabetes. Over 50% of people with hypertension need a combination of two or more drugs to reach their target.
You can read more about comprehensive care plans through the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Guide or review medication classes via the American Heart Association.
